concepts.name: Amphipathic phospholipids form the bilayer
concepts.summary: Phospholipids have a water-loving head and water-avoiding tails, so in water the heads face outward and the tails face inward.

concepts.name: Saturated vs. unsaturated fatty acids
concepts.summary: Saturated tails pack tightly; double bonds in unsaturated tails create kinks that increase fluidity.

concepts.name: What affects membrane fluidity
concepts.summary: Fluidity depends on fatty acid saturation and chain length, temperature, and cholesterol.

concepts.name: Cholesterol as a fluidity buffer
concepts.summary: Cholesterol restricts motion when the membrane is very fluid and keeps it from stiffening when it is cold, widening the transition range.

concepts.name: Fluid mosaic model
concepts.summary: The membrane is a mosaic of lipids, cholesterol and proteins whose components can move sideways (Singer and Nicolson, 1972).

concepts.name: Membrane asymmetry and lipid flipping
concepts.summary: The two leaflets differ in composition; lipids rarely flip between them without enzymes (flippases, floppases, scramblases).

concepts.name: Glycocalyx and cell recognition
concepts.summary: Sugars on the outer surface help cells recognize each other and tell self from non-self.

source_text:
A cell membrane surrounds a cell and regulates exchange with its surroundings. Its phospholipids are amphipathic: each has a hydrophilic (water-loving) head and hydrophobic (water-avoiding) fatty acid tails. In water, they form a bilayer with heads facing water on both sides and tails inside. Each layer is a leaflet.

Fatty acids are carbon chains. Saturated chains lack carbon–carbon double bonds and pack closely. Double bonds in unsaturated tails create bends that hinder packing and increase fluidity. Fluidity means how freely membrane components move. Saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol affect it.

Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it restrains excessive movement and helps prevent cold-induced stiffening. The fluid mosaic model describes a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins with components moving sideways.

The leaflets differ in composition. Lipids seldom switch leaflets unaided; flippases, floppases, and scramblases assist this movement. Outer-surface carbohydrate chains form the glycocalyx, or sugar coating, supporting cell recognition and self/non-self distinction.
